title: Elysium Labs — Dedicated capacity discovery
summary: Discovery focused on sizing a dedicated reserved GPU footprint for Elysium's generative biology inference workloads. Main concerns: tenant isolation, burst handling (warm pools vs. prewarm), eviction tolerance, data residency and KMS integrations. Agreed to run a 2-week pilot with a small reserved pool and benchmark synthetic bursts; Redwood to send pricing and SOC2/KMS docs.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-04
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Blake (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Evan Cho (Redwood CSM); Dr. Lina Cao, Marcus Reed, Anita Patel, Roberto Jimenez (Elysium Labs)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect): Discussed dedicated capacity, required isolation levels for PHI-adjacent models, burst plan. Action items assigned.

[00:00] Jordan Blake: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick roll call -- yeah, so I'm Jordan, AE at Redwood, Priya's our SE, Evan helps with onboarding. Lina, wanna kick off with a bit of background on what Elysium is looking to solve?

[00:18] Dr. Lina Cao: Sure, thanks. Uh hi all. At Elysium we're running a SaaS platform for generative protein design, um heavy inference per request for sequence scoring, folding prompts, so it's a mix of short-chat-like queries and some longer chains, uh typical inference lengths maybe 80 to 1,200 tokens depending on pipeline. We currently run on cloud VMs with model shards on, um, self-hosted GPU infra but it's become operationally heavy. Looking for a predictable per-token cost and lower latency for P50/P95, and of course data controls — we need tenant isolation and KMS.

[00:46] Jordan Blake: Got it. High-level question: are you primarily evaluating Redwood Hosted first or jumping straight to Dedicated / Private?

[00:52] Anita Patel: We're evaluating all three. For initial ramp we want Redwood Hosted to move fast, but our compliance folks want a clear path to Dedicated or Private with VPC and customer KMS — that'll be necessary for some enterprise customers and for regulatory compliance.

[01:06] Priya Nair: That makes sense. For Dedicated we typically provision reserved GPU pools per account with options for warm pools and burst capacity. Before we go deeper — can you share the workload shape? Batch sizes, concurrency, token distribution?

[01:21] Roberto Jimenez: Sure I'll try — our typical live traffic is 120 qps average, spikes to 700 qps during surge windows, each request maybe 300 tokens average; but there are batch jobs that push very long sequences that are more tolerant of latency. So two patterns: real-time low-latency and asynchronous heavy batches.

[01:39] Marcus Reed: Also want to call out multi-tenant risk. We cannot have noisy neighbors; some of our models are considered PHI-adjacent and must not share memory with other teams.

[01:47] Jordan Blake: Understood. On the isolation front Redwood Dedicated supports node-level tenancy and options for single-tenant nodes for strict isolation, and we can do VPC peering or Private deployment for full network separation. I'll note that configuring single-tenant nodes increases cost but reduces blast radius.

[02:04] Dr. Lina Cao: When you say single-tenant nodes, is that whole GPU exclusive? Like we want no shared GPU with other customer jobs.

[02:11] Priya Nair: Yes, we can reserve entire GPU cards for your pool and set tenant fencing. There's also cgroups/namespace isolation at runtime. For the strictest compliance we recommend Private with customer-managed KMS and no egress through public control planes.

[02:26] Marcus Reed: On KMS — we use HashiCorp Vault today and require HSM-backed keys for certain customers. Can Redwood integrate with customer KMS/HSM?

[02:34] Jordan Blake: Yes, Redwood Private supports KMS integrations and HSM-backed flows; Redwood Dedicated can integrate with customer KMS via a VPC path and brokered key wrapping depending on the deployment. We'll include the KMS architecture doc in the follow-up.

[02:47] Evan Cho: Quick doc note — SOC2 and audit logs are available, we can push retention policy specifics in the security pack.

[02:54] Roberto Jimenez: Great. Now about bursts — we've seen huge spikes during release experiments. What's the typical way Redwood handles bursts? Warm pools? Pre-warm nodes? Autoscale?

[03:04] Priya Nair: Good question. We have a couple of levers: 1) Maintain warm pool nodes that keep models loaded (best for lowest cold-start latency), 2) Prewarm runners with model artifacts staged but not fully loaded, and 3) Autoscaling with burst buffers that borrow capacity from a shared burst pool. For Dedicated customers you can configure reserved capacity + a paid burst allowance.

[03:22] Dr. Lina Cao: In our case, cold-starts above 400ms can break user flows. How long to spin up a node from zero to serving?

[03:28] Priya Nair: Cold boot varies by model size and quantization. For example, a 30B quantized model could take 20–45s to fully warm on a GPU. Warm pool nodes keep KV caches primed and the model in GPU memory so p95 jump is minimal. For your latency requirement we recommend a small warm pool sized for your critical path and a fallback policy to a slightly cheaper model variant for less critical calls.

[03:51] Marcus Reed: Fallback policy — you mean automatically route to a quantized variant or smaller architecture if warm pool is exhausted?

[03:56] Priya Nair: Exactly. The router can route by policy: prioritize latency-critical routes to the warm pool, and fall back to cheaper / lower-memory models when capacity is constrained. There's also a regional failover option.

[04:06] Anita Patel: How does that affect token-level costs? Our CFO will ask.

[04:10] Jordan Blake: Cost depends on the model and runtime. Warm pools cost more because GPUs stay allocated; but they dramatically reduce per-request latency and amortize load depending on qps. We'll provide a unit economics sheet that shows per-token cost for warm pool vs cold-start vs fallback to smaller models.

[04:22] Dr. Lina Cao: For the pilot we want to measure three things: p50/p95 latency on our workloads, cost per 1M tokens across steady vs spike, and isolation verification. Is that doable in a 2-week pilot?

[04:33] Priya Nair: Yes — a two-week pilot with a small reserved pool and synthetic burst tests will cover that. We'll need inference traces from you to size the pool and a set of representative prompts.

[04:41] Roberto Jimenez: We can export traces. How do you handle KV cache between prewarm nodes? If requests go to different warm nodes do we lose cache locality?

[04:50] Priya Nair: We shard KV cache per node; for heavy prefix reuse we recommend sticky routing or a small number of hot nodes to reduce cache miss. We can also enable cross-node KV replication for certain workloads, but it adds overhead.

[05:05] Marcus Reed: Eviction tolerance — if a node is preempted for maintenance, what's the glide path? Any warnings or drain process?

[05:12] Priya Nair: Nodes are drained: in-flight requests finish, we mark them as retiring and spin up replacements. For Dedicated reserved pools we offer maintenance windows and options to avoid preemption. For burst pools using spot resources there is higher eviction risk — we recommend not running critical low-latency routes on spot-backed burst nodes.

[05:31] Dr. Lina Cao: Could we have a hybrid: reserved for critical model endpoints, and spot-backed burst nodes for non-critical batch jobs?

[05:37] Jordan Blake: Absolutely, that's a common pattern. Reserve the critical endpoints on Dedicated nodes and configure batch pipelines to run on cheaper burst capacity — Redwood Console can route and show cost breakdown per route.

[05:49] Anita Patel: For pilot SOW — what's included? Benchmarks, config, rollback plan?

[05:55] Evan Cho: Pilot SOW typically covers: reserved pool up to X GPUs (we'll size with your traces), warm pool config, a benchmarking plan (we run synthetic spikes and measure p50/p95), security checklist (SOC2/KMS verification), and a short evaluation report at the end. We'll also include remediation steps and a path for Dedicated -> Private if you decide to move.

[06:14] Roberto Jimenez: Any gotchas on moving to Private later? We have strict network controls and air-gapped requirements for some customers.

[06:20] Priya Nair: Moving to Private requires a brief handoff: a private control plane, VPC setup, KMS connectivity, and optionally an on-prem package. There is an ops handoff but we try to keep the API consistent. Some kernels and optimizations may differ slightly depending on available hardware but we'll profile that in the pilot.

[06:35] Dr. Lina Cao: What about model pinning and rollouts? We need canary testing when updating models in prod.

[06:40] Jordan Blake: Redwood supports version pinning, canary rollouts, and A/B policies. You can bind routes to specific model versions and gradually increase traffic. The Console provides tracing and latency/cost dashboards to monitor regressions.

[06:51] Marcus Reed: One more security note: we need audit logs with token-level redaction and 7-year retention for some customers. Is that standard?

[06:59] Evan Cho: We can accommodate extended retention as an add-on. Audit log redaction for sensitive tokens is supported; we'll include details in the security packet.

[07:09] (short crosstalk)

[07:15] Jordan Blake: Great. Let's recap and assign actions. Lina — you'll share traces and a list of critical endpoints. Roberto — you'll provide SRE constraints like preferred instance types and network CIDRs. We'll send pricing, the pilot SOW, SOC2/KMS docs, and a benchmark template.

[07:33] Dr. Lina Cao: Sounds good. Timeline-wise we'd like the pilot started next week if the SOW lands quickly.

[07:38] Jordan Blake: We'll aim to send the docs in 48 hours. Priya, anything to add?

[07:43] Priya Nair: I'll attach a sample warm-pool config and a checklist for eviction tolerances. Also a sample fallback policy config for routing to quantized variants.

[07:51] Anita Patel: Okay, thanks all.

[07:54] Jordan Blake: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up via email and schedule the kickoff.

[08:00] Meeting end.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings present; some product names mis-transcribed (e.g., KV cache as "K V cache") and Redwood product shorthand as "redwood ded-uh-cated" in auto text.
